[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

review_text_raw:
Picture this: you find a girl's phone, and her name is Anna. But here's the catch - she's missing, and you're the one holding her phone with all its personal information. Creepy, right?

The story revolves around investigating Anna's disappearance, and as you interact with her friends and family through text messages and phone conversations, the tension keeps building up. The drama feels real, and the game's decision-based mechanics force you to make choices that affect the outcome. The best part is, it's not just a mystery unraveling over time; your main goal is clear - find Anna. But beware, Simulacra is not just about jumpscares; it plays with your senses more subtly, with eerie audio effects that might even make you question reality outside the game.

Though the game is quite engaging, it's not without its flaws. The voice acting feels a bit awkward and scripted, and some audio elements seem unnecessary, primarily existing for the sake of providing a jumpscare. But hey, the recorded videos are well done, especially Anna's personal vlogs.

Playing this game on PC might not be as immersive as on a mobile phone but it holds its merit reguardless. Still, they could've allowed portrait mode like in Downwell to make it even better.

All in all, Simulacra is a decent horror title that excels in subtle horror and decision-based gameplay. It really makes you think about privacy, honesty, and data security, and that's something you don't often get from a horror game. So, if you're up for an unnerving experience that's a bit different from the usual horror games, give Simulacra a try!

This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones.

There's a sub-genre of games that I like to call voyeur sims -- these include walking simulators like Gone Home, strategy-puzzlers like the Orwell games, and story-driven phone-sim games like [b]SIMULACRA[/b].

These voyeur sims fuel something visceral in me by allowing me to be a peeping tom in someone else's life; overcoming personal privacy as a game mechanic is somehow uncomfortably fun, even when the actual gameplay is minimal.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is one of the better voyeur sims and one of the better games I've played this year. Like other phone-sim games like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/523210/A_Normal_Lost_Phone/]A Normal Lost Phone[/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/496890/Replica/]Replica[/url], it starts with a mysterious cell phone, and throughout the game, you unpack its content in a series of puzzle-driven unlocking sequences.

What sets [b]SIMULACRA[/b] apart is its high production value. High quality FMVs, passable and explorable versions of popular social media apps, realistic text logs and emails -- these all make the small, contained world of [b]SIMULACRA[/b] believable and immersive.

This is a great game. Recommended.

Interesting and thought-provoking story, with a compelling, mysterious vibe.

Can be beaten in less than 4 hours, and then a 2nd playthrough can be done much faster, thanks to a faster story mode.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is essentially a found footage film but as a game.
One day someone leaves you a phone at your doorstep, which belongs to a girl that has gone missing.
From there, it's your job to snoop through her phone to uncover hints on what happened to her.
The actors can be very cheesy and hardly believable, but that has it's own charm if you are into that kind of thing. The problem I had with the story was the horror elements that they try to shove in, in the form of jump scares. Apart from being the annoying type of jump scares, they also immediately take the story in a direction, where you as the player know where the story will end up. If the jump scares where replaced with more subtle hints that something is off, I think it would have been a lot more engaging.
  
To give credit to the devs, they did a good job at imitating a phone OS with  multiple apps. That makes it fun to snoop around for clues on how to gain access to specific parts of the phone. Even though you have a variety of apps to explore, however, multitasking is something that the fake OS lacks, which makes jumping back and forth from different apps a chore. Having to constantly scroll through everything to get to the part you need can quickly become a nuisance, especially when it deletes the things you have to fill in.

Despite these issues, I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it for the price. It only takes around 3 to 4 hours to finish, but it has multiple endings. A new game plus mode exists, which fast-forwards the conversations. I wish it would skip the puzzles as well, so you can just focus on the endings, but alas, it is what it is.

This game asks a lot of the player. The morality of digging through someone's privacy to maybe find that person is always a great hook when the stakes seem so low. As the game progresses you find yourself making more and more of these judgement calls. Until, in the end, you're left wondering whether or not you've done anything right. You probably haven't. So reboot and start again.

A game worth playing a few times.

I'm gonna recommend the game because there's not many out there like this, so I hope more get made.

It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.

A psychological horror/mystery about invading others privacy and cyberstalking?  Talk about checking all my boxes at once!  I'm in!!!

Okay, so this is a little game about you having someone elses cellphone.  I beat it in a few hours, four maybe, and enjoyed the trip.  Everything you have to do in this game, you do with this cell phone.  You get to break into email accounts, search online registries for sex offenders, and catfish people, all in an attempt to find the ultimate truth.  It's like someone finally based a game off my hobbies.

So, the story is kind of linear, in that you work to unlock new areas of the mystery, piece by piece.  First, you get to play with texts and pictures, then you get enough information to open the email, then you can gather what you need to beat security questions...  I'd say the gameplay is about sifting through information to find what you need to move on.  You also get to talk to the phone owner's friends, and they help to move the plot along, or you can ask them for help if you get stuck.

I say it's linear, but there are actually several branching paths that probably all end up in the same place.  Do you know Telltale games?  Kind of like that...  We might make a different turn here and there, but we're all on the same road with a beginning, middle and end.  Example?  Okay, here's an example...  You need to find out some information from this person through text.  Do you own up, tell them you're a creepo reading through someone elses phone because they might be in trouble, or do you try to bluff your way through, pretending to be who you're not?  Make your choice and either way, life will go on.  I don't think you can get stuck.  Then at the end they have a nice little screen that says things like "You and 68% of players looked at the porn stash," just like a Telltale game.  (there was no porn stash...)

It's pretty creative storywise, and I'm not going to give anything away, but it looked like there were about 4 different endings, and I wouldn't be adverse to trying again sometime to see how things can change.  I only had two of them available to me, so I must have needed to do something else to unlock the others, and I'm not entirely sure what that is, which is good to me.  Means the game still has more meat to it.  It reminded me of another game I played called Her Story, and I didn't recommend that one because one play is all it's good for, but this one was more than double the length and I'd be happy to go again some day.

Scariness, it wasn't scary, but I'm pretty tough to phase.  It likes to make creepy noises in your headphones.  There's some image distortion, but I wouldn't call anything a jump scare, which is good, because those turn people off.

TL:DR I had fun.  Maybe you'll have fun too?  I hope I've given you enough information to know if you'll enjoy it too.  That's why I'm writing all this after all.

Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

You've obtained the phone of a missing woman named Anna. Your goal is to snoop around her phone's files, social media, and her contacts to get more information about who may have taken her. 

The game simulates what it's like to be in this situation very well with the phone and notification sounds. It feels both dangerous and scandalous at the same time. Like at any moment, police will be knocking on your door asking why you have her phone. 

I actually got a bit invested in figuring out what was going on, but I also wanted to be a terrible person and mislead people to see what would happen. 

Who are you relative to the situation? 
Maybe you're the one who kidnapped her! 
Play the game to see for yourself because I do recommend it.

The main thing dragging back the game isn't the story. It's not the immoral conversations you are having with Anna's abusive ex boyfriend, Greg. It's not even about the advice you're taking from register sex offender, Taylor. 

It's just the cringe acting. 

Honestly that's it. 

The acting is awful, like really acting. Anna sounds like she's reading from a script. Same applies to all characters. From Taylor's singing to Greg cursing you out, these people cannot act.

Another issue is investment in the characters, I don't like any of them so I don't feel for any of them. 

Also the characters are stupid, simply stupid. None of them decide to ever call you out for being a potential suspect, and only one calls the cops after a while.

I'm not a fan of horror genre. I find stupid main characters hard to root for, and just like horror movies on Netflix, I've lowered my expectations to just enjoy the slop.

It's a well put together game, with a believable UI for a Samsung phone.

I've never played a game quite like this before, and for that alone I will recommend it. You basically have the phone of a missing girl and attempt to rescue/find out what happened to her by snooping through her phone. You slowly get access to more and more features of her phone (sometimes in really clever ways, like figuring out her password to an app). Slowly a horror plot unfolds as you find out more and more about what happened.

* Choices that matter (multiple endings)

Best played without "scouting" the plot online first; the villain reveal is much more interesting this way.

review_text_raw:
An unsettling narrative that employs our intuitive knowledge of phones as a framework for oddly intuitive deductions and uncanny subversions.

It’s not a wholly unique concept for horror, but plenty of what’s done through interaction distinguishes Simulacra from the other cursed-PC or texting-based games with an opinion about digital privacy. Even if my thoughts were first drawn to comparisons, the strength of that initial ambiguity set within the benign familiarity of a mobile OS had me playing along in no time.

While the fixation on relationship drama does drive the story, it also seems to conflict with Simulacra's insidious tone. Although, the seemingly necessary overindulgence in others’ personal affairs does heighten a different sense of uneasiness. When the pixels aren't going "boo", Simulacra can be immensely unnerving. Silent realizations even provoked chills on more than one occasion.

Even if the narrative isn't unexpectedly divergent, the amount of time I spent mulling over the game's events speaks to the impact that they had on my participation. There's a lot to unwrap here and no better way to learn more than to play it for yourself.

What would you do if a stranger left their phone at your doorstep? Would you try to unlock it and snoop around? Of course you would! And this is the story of Simulacra.

This is a strait forward puzzle game where one has to dig through a stranger’s phone, and talk to third parties through their device, to unlock the mystery of their disappearance. Additional play throughs are sped up with a “Begin +” mode; Which makes messages appear faster but there are a ton of unskippable moments that make achievement hunting a chore. That second, and third, play through was rough… 

Worth  a couple bucks for a single play through, but, regardless of ending, it’s painful to get through multiple times. If there was a way to skip the redundancy, this would have been a perfect achievement hunters’ game.

Either way, yeah... Simulacra is a solid adventure game for a cheap price. Check it out.

Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10
